summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of spinal gunshot wound, neurogenic bladder, and chronic indwelling catheter was admitted for left-sided back pain, fevers, and chills concerning for pyelonephritis. She also reported a productive cough and hoarseness. Initial labs showed leukocytosis, and urinalysis indicated infection. Blood cultures were negative. Urine culture grew ESBL-producing E. coli, resistant to most antibiotics but sensitive to nitrofurantoin, tobramycin, and meropenem. Given clinical improvement on initial therapy and resolution of fever, she was diagnosed with bacterial cystitis rather than pyelonephritis. She was transitioned to oral nitrofurantoin for outpatient treatment. A primary care appointment was arranged, and she was counseled on the benefits of a suprapubic catheter to reduce infection risk. She was also advised about the health risks of ongoing cocaine use. She improved clinically, remained afebrile, and was discharged home with instructions to complete antibiotics and obtain a follow-up urine culture.
